text: dsh-bash-guardrails 是面向 DSH 的 bash 命令规则插件：它在 bash 工具调用执行前解析命令，并按内置或自定义规则决定是否拦截。插件通过前置工具监听器检查调用，并用同步 guard 作为补充；规则可针对语法解析失败、从根目录开始的 find、pgrep/pkill、循环等待以及文件读写类命令。规则开关可在插件配置中设置，自定义规则可放在用户或项目的 JSON 文件中，使用 CEL 表达式描述条件。适合希望在 DSH 工作流中统一约束 bash 调用并给出替代操作提示的用户。源码未配置 API key 或外部服务。

dsh-bash-guardrails checks DSH bash calls before execution and denies calls matching built-in or custom rules. It parses commands and applies configurable CEL rules from JSON files. It helps enforce consistent bash checks in DSH.
想让 DSH 在运行 bash 命令前先检查是否符合我设置的规则。
怎样阻止 agent 用某些 bash 命令，并告诉它改用合适的文件工具？
I want DSH to parse shell commands and deny calls that match configurable rules.
dsh-bash-guardrails 的功能「bash 规则检查」：在 bash 工具执行前解析调用并依序评估内置及自定义规则；命中时拒绝调用并返回原因，未命中则继续执行。
dsh-bash-guardrails 的功能「自定义 CEL 规则」：从用户目录和当前项目目录读取 JSON 规则文件，将 CEL 条件编译为规则，并在文件变化后重新加载；可用于增加项目特定的 bash 拦截条件。

dsh-bash-guardrails README · dsh-bash-guardrails：A [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness) (DSH) plugin that enforces **guard rules on bash tool calls**. Before the agent runs a `bash` command, the plugin checks it against a set of rules and, if one matches, blocks the call with a short explanation so the agent can correct course on its own. Each built-in rule is a toggle, and only two are on by default. You can add your own rules, written in [CEL](https://cel.dev), in the same format the built-in rules use.

dsh-bash-guardrails README · dsh-bash-guardrails：It is a port of [cc-bash-guardrails](https://github.com/ruihe774/cc-bash-guardrails) (a Claude Code mod), sharing its rule engine, shell analysis and rule-file format. Requires DSH 0.2.1-rc.5 or a later 0.2 release.

dsh-bash-guardrails README · Why not Auto review or a regex hook?：**Auto review.** DSH's experimental Auto review asks a model whether an action is *unsafe or unauthorized*. The pitfalls here are different: commands that are allowed and not malicious but reliably waste time or cause trouble, such as `find /` crawling the whole filesystem, `pgrep -f` matching the harness's own helper processes, or an `until grep` loop that never exits when the writer dies. These rules are deterministic, so the same command is always handled the same way, and each denial tells the agent what to do instead. They work alongside Auto review (see [below](#with-auto-review)).
section: Why not Auto review or a regex hook?

text: dsh-bash-guardrails README · Why not Auto review or a regex hook?：**Regex hooks.** Matching the command text with a regular expression is brittle in both directions. `echo "find / -name x"` trips a regex for `find /`, while `cd /x && find / -name y`, `bash -c "find / -type f"`, `echo $(find /)`, `\sudo ls` or `env X=1 timeout 5 find /` slip past a simple one. This plugin parses the command with a real shell parser (a vendored copy of [unbash](https://github.com/webpro-nl/unbash)) and checks the commands that would actually run, so quoting, escapes, pipelines, `&&` chains, subshells, command substitutions, heredocs and `bash -c` strings are all understood. Commands behind wrappers such as `env`, `timeout`, `nice`, `xargs`, `sudo` and `run0` are checked too.
section: Why not Auto review or a regex hook?

text:
dsh-bash-guardrails README · What it does：| Rule | Default | Blocks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `malformed_bash` | on | Bash commands that fail to parse. The agent gets the parse error and retries. The other rules rely on the parse: with this rule off, a command that doesn't parse may be only partly checked. |
| `find_root` | on | `find` rooted at `/` (including `//`, `/*` and `find -- /`), even with `-xdev`. It is independent of `find_xdev`. |
| `find_xdev` | off | `find` without `-xdev` or `-mount` (or BSD/macOS `-x`), so searches never cross filesystem boundaries. `find --help` and `--version` are left alone. |
| `pgrep_f` | off | `pgrep -f` without `-a`, and any `pkill -f`. `-f` can match helper processes spawned by the harness, and `pkill` would kill them; `pgrep -af` shows each command line so matches can be verified before killing by PID. |
| `pgrep_captured` | off | `pgrep` output captured by a pipe or substitution (`pgrep x \| wc -l`, `$(pgrep x)`, `<(pgrep x)`). |
| `until_grep` | off | `until grep ...` and `while ! grep ...` loops (also `egrep`, `fgrep` and `rg`), which never exit if the process writing the log dies. The agent is pointed to `tail -f --pid=<PID> <log> \| grep

dsh-bash-guardrails README · What it does：Every rule is checked in the order above, then your [custom rules](#custom-rules), and the first match decides. A denied call does not run; the agent sees `Error: <reason> No commands in this tool call have been run.` Anything no rule matches runs as usual.

These rules are meant to catch common mistakes, not to be a security boundary. A command assembled at run time (`$cmd`, `eval "$x"`) or run through a program that is not a recognized wrapper (`ssh host find /`, `watch find /`) is not seen.

dsh-bash-guardrails README · When it runs：- On every `bash` tool call: calls the model makes directly, `bash` calls inside a PTC `run_code` program, and calls made by in-process subagents.
- Other tools are never touched. `pwsh` and the interactive `terminal` tool are not checked.
- If the check itself fails, the call is blocked rather than run unchecked.

dsh-bash-guardrails README · With Auto review：The check is a `tools/pre-execute` listener kept **in front of** every other one, Auto review included:

- A call a rule denies never reaches the reviewer: no review request, no tokens, no approval prompt, and the agent gets the rule's explanation rather than a generic review denial.
- A call no rule denies goes on to Auto review exactly as before.

dsh-bash-guardrails README · With Auto review：Cordis runs the most recently prepended listener first, and Auto review prepends its listener when it is switched on, which can be after this plugin. So whenever another plugin prepends a `tools/pre-execute` listener, this plugin re-registers its own in front. Correctness doesn't depend on that ordering: a denial further down the chain still wins in Auto review, and a `ctx.tools.guard()` backstop denies a matching call even if some listener ahead of this one allows without passing it on. If two plugins kept fighting for first place, this one stops after 20 attempts in a second and logs a warning, and the guard still applies.

dsh-bash-guardrails README · Installation：From a checkout:

```sh
npm install
npm run build
```

Then install the directory into your DSH profile, from the Web UI's plugin manager or with the CLI:

```sh
dsh plugin --profile web add /path/to/dsh-bash-guardrails
```

dsh-bash-guardrails README · Configuration：Each built-in rule is a boolean option on the plugin row, named as in the table above (`sudo`, `find_xdev`, …). Only `malformed_bash` and `find_root` default to `true`. Change them in your profile's patch layer (`~/.dsh/profiles/<profile>/cordis.patch.yml`). An override replaces the row's whole `config`, and options you leave out keep their defaults:

```yaml
- id: bash-guardrails
  name: dsh-bash-guardrails
  config:
    find_xdev: true

dsh-bash-guardrails README · Custom rules：| Field | |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | Required. Letters, digits, `-` and `_`. It can't be a built-in rule's id. |
| `when` | Required. A [CEL](https://cel.dev) expression that must be a `bool`. The rule fires when it is `true`. |
| `deny` | Required. The reason the agent sees when the rule blocks the call. |
| `let` | Optional. Named CEL values, in order, that `when`, the message and later `let`s can use. |
| `tools` | Optional. `["bash"]`, the default and only tool. `Bash` is accepted as an alias, and `Monitor` (a Claude Code tool) is ignored, so rule files written for cc-bash-guardrails load unchanged. |
| `enabled` | Optional. `false` turns the rule off. |

dsh-bash-guardrails README · Custom rules：`deny` is a template: `{{ expr }}` inserts the value of a CEL expression. There is no `allow` action: a custom rule can only make the guard stricter, so a project's rule file can at worst block calls, and can't turn off a built-in rule or one of yours.

`ask` rules (asking the user before a call runs) are not supported yet. A rule with `ask` is skipped and reported when its file loads.

dsh-bash-guardrails README · What a rule sees：| Name | Type | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `tool` | `string` | `bash` |
| `input` | `map<string, dyn>` | The tool's input: `command`, `description`, `workdir`, `run_in_background` |
| `cmds` | `list<Cmd>` | Every simple command the shell would run, including those in pipelines, `&&` chains, subshells, substitutions, `bash -c` strings and behind wrappers such as `env`, `timeout`, `xargs`, `sudo` and `run0` |
| `errors` | `list<string>` | Parse errors. When it isn't empty, `cmds` may be incomplete. |
| `untilConds` | `list<list<Cmd>>` | For each `until` or `while !` loop, the commands of its condition |
| `pipelines` | `list<list<Cmd>>` | For each pipeline (`a \| b \| c`), its stages in order. A stage that is not a simple command, such as `{ ...; }`, has `name` `''`. |
| your `defs` | | Constants from the file's `defs`, and the built-in ones (`FIND_LEAD`, `FIND_EXPR`, `PGREP`, `GREPS`, `CAT`, `HEAD_TAIL`, `SED`, `AWK`, `TEE`, `PYTHON` and the others in [`src/builtin-rules.ts`](src/builtin-rules.ts)) |

dsh-bash-guardrails README · What a rule sees：A `Cmd` has `name` (the program's basename), `args` (its arguments, with quotes removed), `captured` (its output goes into a pipe or a substitution), `wrappers` (the wrappers in front of it, outermost first, including those in front of a shell running it, as in `sudo sh -c "..."`) and `chain`, a list of `Link`s, one for each wrapper's invocation and a last one for the command itself. A `Link` has `name` (the program's basename) and `argv` (its invocation as written, the program's path included). So `env X=1 sudo -u root ls -l` has `name` `ls`, `args` `["-l"]`, and a `chain` of `env`, `sudo` and `ls` whose `argv`s are `["env", "X=1", "sudo", "-u", "root", "ls", "-l"]`, `["sudo", "-u", "root", "ls", "-l"]` and `["ls", "-l"]`.

dsh-bash-guardrails README · What a rule sees：A `Cmd` also has `redirects`, a list of `Redir`s: its own, then those of the compound commands around it (`{ ...; } > f`, `for ...; done > f`) and of a shell running it (`bash -c "..." > f`), innermost first. A `Redir` has `op` (`>`, `>>`, `<`, `<<`, `<<-`, `<<<`, `>&`, `&>` and so on), `fd` (the descriptor written before the operator, `-1` if none, `-2` for a `{var}` one), `target` (the file, descriptor or here-string word, or a heredoc's delimiter), `body` (the text a heredoc or here-string feeds in, or `''`) and `quoted` (a heredoc whose delimiter is quoted, so its body is not expanded). And `stdout` is where those redirects send its output: a file, `&2` for another descriptor, or `''` when it is not redirected.

dsh-bash-guardrails README · What a rule sees：On top of [standard CEL](https://github.com/google/cel-spec/blob/master/doc/langdef.md), including macros such as `exists`, `all`, `filter` and `map`, `cel.bind`, and `matches` for regular expressions (JavaScript syntax), rules can use:

dsh-bash-guardrails README · What a rule sees：| Function | |
| --- | --- |
| `args.opts(spec)`, `args.operands(spec)` | Parse a `list<string>` of arguments by a spec and return the options seen, or the operands. A spec is a map with any of: `short` (getopt letters, a `:` after one that takes a value, `::` after one whose value is optional and only in the same argument, as `-i.bak`), `shortTakesValue` (every letter in `short` takes a value, and only from the same argument), `long` (long option names mapped to the name to report, as `{"full": "f"}`; a name ending in `:`, as `{"expression": "e:"}`, takes a value from `=value` or else the next argument), `words` (find-style words, each mapped to how many arguments follow it, or to a list of terminators as `{"-exec": [";", "+"]}`), `wordPatterns` (the same, keyed by regex) and `posix` (stop at the first operand). |
| `args.optValues(spec, name)` | The values given to option `name` (as reported by `opts`), in order: `['-e', 'a', '-eb'].optValues({"short": "e:"}, 'e')` is `["a", "b"]` |
| `list.takeWhile(regex)` | The leading items that match the regex |
| `list.take(n)`, `list.drop(n)` | The first `n` items; all but the first `n` |
| `sh
dsh-bash-guardrails README · What a rule sees：The built-in rules in [`src/builtin-rules.ts`](src/builtin-rules.ts) are written the same way, so they are worked examples.

dsh-bash-guardrails README · When rules load, and when they fail：A rule file is read when a session starts and again whenever it changes (by modification time and size), so edits apply to the next call without a restart. Each rule is type-checked when it loads: a typo such as `c.nmae`, `cmds.name == 'find'` (a list has no `name`) or a `when` that isn't a `bool` is caught there. A rule, def or file that fails to load is skipped, and a warning in the DSH host log names it and the error; the other rules keep working. A rule that fails while it runs, for example on a malformed argument spec, blocks the call.
section: When rules load, and when they fail

text:
dsh-bash-guardrails README · What it runs, sends, and fetches：- It runs inside the DSH host process: a `tools/pre-execute` listener, a tool guard, and an `agent/created` listener that loads the rule files early so problems are reported when a session starts.
- It makes **no model calls**, **no network requests**, and **no shell commands**. Commands are only parsed, never executed.
- It reads only its two rule files and writes no files. To find the first, it reads `DSH_HOME` and your home directory.
- It logs the id of each rule that denies a call (not the command) and rule-file problems to the host log. It does not collect, store, or transmit any data.
- Its dependencies are vendored and have no install step: the [unbash](https://github.com/webpro-nl/unbash) parser (ISC license, in `src/vendor/unbash/`) and the [cel-js](https://github.com/marcbachmann/cel-js) CEL interpreter (MIT license, bundled into `src/vendor/cel/`). At run time it imports only `@deepseek-ai/schemastery`, which DSH supplies.
section: What it runs, sends, and fetches

text: dsh-bash-guardrails README · Development：The rule logic is pure and kept free of the DSH API: the CEL engine (`compileFile`, `decide` and `decideDenySync`) in `src/engine.ts`, the argument parser in `src/argv.ts`, and the parser wrapper `analyze` in `src/shell.ts`. The built-in rules are data in `src/builtin-rules.ts`, compiled in `src/rules.ts`. `src/rule-files.ts` loads the rule files, `src/keep-first.ts` keeps the listener in front, and `src/index.ts` is the plugin (`name`, `inject`, `Config`, `apply`). `src/dsh.ts` mirrors the few DSH types used.

dsh-bash-guardrails README · Development：```sh
npm test          # compiles to .test-out and runs node --test
npm run typecheck
npm run build     # src -> lib
```

`tests/rules.test.ts` covers the built-in rules, `tests/engine.test.ts` custom rules and the engine, and `tests/plugin.test.ts` the plugin on the real DSH tool pipeline (`@deepseek-ai/dsh-tools` 0.2.1-rc.5), including ordering against a later prepended listener in Auto review's shape.
